questions.topic: Returning Multiple Results — Pass by Pointer
questions.q: How to properly design a mathematical calculation function if you need to calculate and return two values at once (for example, minimum and maximum from an array)?
questions.hint: Since return in C can only return a single value, what mechanism is used to pass alternative outputs?
options: Pass pointers to variables for results into function parameters and write calculations to those addresses
Use two return statements in a row: return min; return max;
Pass results through global variable errno
Create an array inside the function and return its local address
explanations: Correct! Passing pointers in function parameters (`void get_min_max(..., int *out_min, int *out_max)`) is the standard way to return multiple calculated results in C.
Incorrect. The first executed `return` will immediately terminate the function.
Incorrect. The `errno` variable is intended exclusively for system error codes, not for regular calculation results.
Incorrect. Returning the address of a local array will lead to a dangling pointer and Undefined Behavior.

questions.q: Why is it recommended to use const Vector *v instead of Vector v when passing a large structure (for example, a $4 \times 4$ matrix or a 3D grid) into a mathematical calculation function?
questions.hint: Compare pass-by-value and pass-by-pointer in terms of resource consumption and data protection.
options: Passing by `const` pointer avoids expensive copying of the entire structure onto the stack and protects it from accidental modification
Pass-by-value is strictly forbidden by the compiler for any structures
The `const` qualifier speeds up CPU performance by 10 times
A pointer automatically offloads calculations to the graphics card (GPU)
explanations: Correct! Passing `Vector v` by value performs a byte-for-byte copy of all structure fields onto the stack. Using `const Vector *v` passes only an address (8 bytes on a 64-bit system), and `const` guarantees that the calculation function will not modify the original data.
Incorrect. Passing structures by value is completely allowed in C, but inefficient for large objects.
Incorrect. `const` helps the compiler and protects code, but does not inherently speed up work by a fixed factor.
Incorrect. Offloading calculations to a GPU requires specific frameworks (OpenCL, CUDA).

questions.q: Why pass a parameter like double (*math_func)(double) to a numerical integration function (for example, computing an integral using the trapezoidal rule)?
questions.hint: Does this allow making the algorithm universal for different functions $f(x)$?
options: So that the integration algorithm can compute the integral of any mathematical function $f(x)$ passed as an argument
To speed up function calculation at compile time
This is the only way to pass real numbers of type double into functions
So that the integration function can modify the source code of the mathematical function
explanations: Correct! Passing a function pointer allows abstracting a mathematical algorithm (integration, root finding, differentiation) from a specific formula $f(x)$.
Incorrect. Calling via a function pointer instead creates an indirect call at runtime.
Incorrect. Regular `double` numbers are passed directly by value.
Incorrect. Function code in execution memory resides in a read-only section (`.text`).

questions.topic: Passing Arrays — Loss of Size Information
questions.q: Why is it mandatory to pass the size `size` as a separate parameter to an array summation function `double sum(const double *arr, size_t size)`?
questions.hint: What happens to an array when its name is passed as a function argument?
options: The array name decays to a pointer to the first element, and the function has no information about the array length
C forbids passing arrays without specifying a size parameter of type `size_t` at the end
Array size is automatically determined via `sizeof(arr)` inside the function
This is required only for arrays of negative numbers
explanations: Correct! In C, when an array is passed as a function parameter, it degrades to a regular pointer to the element type (`const double *`). All information about the number of elements is lost (Array decay), so the length `size` must be passed explicitly.
Incorrect. The order and presence of parameters is defined by the programmer, but without size, loop iteration becomes impossible.
Incorrect. Inside the function, `sizeof(arr)` will return the size of the pointer itself (4 or 8 bytes), not the entire array.
Incorrect. This rule applies to arrays of any types and values.

questions.q: Which function from <stdlib.h> calculates both the quotient and remainder of integer division simultaneously and returns them as a div_t structure?
questions.hint: The function name matches the mathematical division operation.
options: div()
mod()
quotient()
split_div()
explanations: Correct! The `div(int numer, int denom)` function computes the quotient and remainder in a single operation and returns a `div_t` structure containing fields `quot` (quotient) and `rem` (remainder).
Incorrect. The remainder operation in C is the `%` operator or the `fmod()` function for `double`.
Incorrect. The `quotient()` function does not exist in the standard library.
Incorrect. The `split_div()` function is absent in C.

questions.q: Which of the following function headers is valid for receiving a $3 \times 3$ two-dimensional array (matrix) to calculate its determinant?
questions.hint: Which dimension must be explicitly specified to the compiler to calculate memory strides?
options: double det(double m[][3])
double det(double m[][])
double det(double [][]m)
double det(double *m[3][3])
explanations: Correct! When passing multidimensional arrays, the C compiler requires the length of all dimensions except the first (in this case `[3]`) to correctly compute element addresses `m[i][j]` using the formula `i * cols + j`.
Incorrect. Writing `double m[][]` will cause a compilation error because the compiler cannot determine the row size.
Incorrect. Such bracket syntax is invalid in C.
Incorrect. Writing `double *m[3][3]` declares a two-dimensional array of pointers, not an array of `double` numbers.

questions.topic: Returning Values — Complex and Composite Numbers via struct
questions.q: How does the function `Complex add_complex(Complex a, Complex b)`, which returns the result of adding two complex numbers as a structure, behave?
questions.hint: What happens to a returned object of type struct?
options: The returned structure is copied entirely by value to the calling code
A pointer to a structure on the heap is automatically created
The compiler forbids returning structures from calculation functions
The structure is destroyed before the calling code has time to read it
explanations: Correct! In C, functions can return structures by value. The returned instance is copied into the calling function's context (often via ABI optimization using special registers).
Incorrect. Heap memory is not allocated automatically.
Incorrect. Returning structures is fully supported by the C standard.
Incorrect. A copy of the return value is created before the stack frame is destroyed.

questions.topic: Variadic Functions — Calculating Unknown Length Parameters
questions.q: Why is the count parameter passed first when calculating the sum of numbers in a variadic function `double sum(int count, ...)`?
questions.hint: Does the `...` function know the number of arguments passed into it by itself?
options: The variadic argument mechanism in C does not track argument count, so it must be passed explicitly
This is a requirement of the mathematical library for formatting
The first parameter `count` is automatically calculated by the preprocessor
Without `count`, the function cannot return a `double` value
explanations: Correct! The variadic list `...` contains no information about the number or types of arguments. Passing the count (or a sentinel terminator) is necessary so the `va_arg` loop knows when to stop reading from the stack.
Incorrect. This is a general C rule for any variadic functions, not just mathematical ones.
Incorrect. The preprocessor does not count function call arguments.
Incorrect. The return type is completely unrelated to the `count` parameter.

questions.topic: Optimization — restrict Qualifier in Vector Calculations
questions.q: What advantage does adding the restrict qualifier to pointers provide in an element-wise vector addition function `void add_vectors(size_t n, double * restrict a, const double * restrict b)`?
questions.hint: Can vector memory regions overlap, and how does this affect SIMD vectorization?
options: Guarantees that memory regions `a` and `b` do not overlap, allowing the compiler to apply SIMD loop vectorization
Makes the function thread-safe
Automatically computes vector size at compile time
Forbids passing NaN values into the function
explanations: Correct! `restrict` promises the compiler that pointers `a` and `b` do not refer to overlapping memory regions (no aliasing). This allows the compiler's auto-vectorizer to unroll the loop using fast vector instructions (AVX/NEON).
Incorrect. `restrict` affects pointer aliasing, not thread synchronization.
Incorrect. Vector size is passed via `size_t n` at runtime.
Incorrect. `restrict` does not affect checking for NaN values.

questions.q: Which calculation function is called a 'Pure function' and permits optimization by eliminating redundant calls with identical arguments?
questions.hint: Do such functions depend on global variables or modify external state?
options: A function whose result depends ONLY on passed arguments and has no side effects
A function written without using pointers
A function that accepts only `int` type arguments
A function containing no `for` or `while` loops inside
explanations: Correct! A pure function always returns the same result for identical input arguments and does not modify global state (no side effects). The compiler can optimize code by replacing repeated calls to `f(x)` with a previously saved result.
Incorrect. Using pointers (especially with the `const` qualifier) does not prevent a function from being pure.
Incorrect. Parameter types do not affect the concept of function purity.
Incorrect. The presence of loops in no way contradicts the concept of a pure function.

questions.topic: return Statement — Early Exit from void Function
questions.q: Can a return statement be used without specifying a value inside a function with return type void?
questions.hint: Think about how to interrupt function execution before it reaches the end of its last line.
options: Yes, return; is used for early exit and terminating void function execution
No, in void functions the return statement is strictly forbidden
Yes, but only if written as return 0;
No, a function is always required to reach the closing brace }
explanations: Correct! The `return;` instruction (without an expression) immediately terminates a `void` function and returns control to the call site.
Incorrect. `return;` is completely legal in `void` functions and is often used to check boundary conditions at the beginning of a function.
Incorrect. Writing `return 0;` in a `void` function causes a compilation error because the function must not return a value.
Incorrect. Early exit is a standard control flow pattern.

questions.q: Does standard C support default parameter values (for example, void print_num(int x = 10))?
questions.hint: Recall if this feature from C++ is available in pure C.
options: No, C has no syntax for default parameter values
Yes, it is a standard feature of C and C++
Yes, but only for int type arguments
Yes, if the argument is marked as static
explanations: Correct! Unlike C++, pure C does not support default parameter values. All arguments declared in a function prototype must be explicitly passed upon calling.
Incorrect. This feature exists in C++, but is absent in C.
Incorrect. The `int x = 10` syntax in a C parameter list causes a compiler error regardless of type.
Incorrect. The `static` modifier cannot be applied to function parameters in this manner.

questions.q: If int x = 5; is declared inside main(), and int x = 20; is declared inside function foo(), how will they interact?
questions.hint: Do local variables with identical names in different functions affect each other?
options: These are two completely separate variables located in different memory regions; they do not affect each other in any way
A compilation error will occur due to redeclaring variable x
The variable in foo() will overwrite the variable value in main()
The variable x value in main() will automatically become equal to 20
explanations: Correct! Each function creates its own scope (stack frame). The `x` variables are completely independent and stored in different memory locations.
Incorrect. Redeclaration error occurs only when creating two variables with the same name inside the same scope.
Incorrect. Function `foo()` works only with its own local `x`.
Incorrect. Variable `x` in `main()` will retain its value of 5.

questions.q: Is it allowed to pass specific numbers directly into a function instead of variables (for example, sum(10, 20))?
questions.hint: Does it matter to a function whether it is passed a variable holding 10 or the number 10 itself?
options: Yes, any expressions including constants and literals can be passed as arguments
No, only pre-created variables can be passed
Yes, but only if passed through pointers first
No, C requires creating variables for every call
explanations: Correct! Because parameters are passed by value, the compiler only cares about the evaluated value of the type (in this case `int`), so calls `sum(10, 20)` and `sum(a, b)` are completely valid.
Incorrect. Storing numbers in intermediate variables before calling is optional.
Incorrect. Pointers do not need to be applied to literals.
Incorrect. Direct passing of literals is one of the most common function usage patterns.

questions.q: What will happen to variable num in main() if passed to function void add_one(int val) { val = val + 1; }?
questions.hint: Recall the fundamental rule of pass-by-value parameters.
options: Variable num in main() will NOT change because the function modified only its local copy val
Variable num will increase by 1
A runtime error will occur
Variable num will be set to zero
explanations: Correct! When passing by value, `add_one` receives a copy of `num`'s content. Modifying local parameter `val` inside `add_one` does not affect the original `num`.
Incorrect. To change the original, the variable address `&num` would need to be passed.
Incorrect. This is a completely standard and safe operation.
Incorrect. The original value remains unchanged.

questions.topic: Syntax Synonyms — void Specifier in Parameter List
questions.q: What does specifying the word void in parameter list void say_hi(void) guarantee in C?
questions.hint: How does `foo(void)` differ from `foo()` in classic C standards?
options: Strictly guarantees that the function takes no arguments
Means the function takes one argument of unspecified type
Instructs compiler to make function virtual
This is obsolete syntax that does not compile
explanations: Correct! In C, `void func(void)` explicitly informs the compiler that the function accepts zero arguments. Historically, `void func()` meant the function accepts an *unspecified* number of arguments.
Incorrect. For unspecified types, `void*` or variadic arguments `...` are used.
Incorrect. There is no concept of virtual functions in C.
Incorrect. This is the standard and correct way to declare parameterless functions in C.

questions.topic: Concepts — Printing to Screen vs Returning Value
questions.q: What is the fundamental difference between calling printf() inside a function and using return statement?
questions.hint: Can the calling program use text simply printed to console?
options: printf() only prints text to the screen (side effect), while return passes the result back to the program for further calculations
There is no difference, both options pass data into main()
return works only with strings, and printf() only with numbers
printf() terminates function execution, while return does not
explanations: Correct! Terminal output via `printf()` is visible to the user, but the calling function does not receive this data. The `return` statement gives the computed value back to the program so it can be stored in a variable or used in a formula.
Incorrect. Displaying in console and returning value to register/stack are fundamentally different things.
Incorrect. Both `return` and `printf` can work with any data types.
Incorrect. On the contrary: `return` terminates function, while `printf` simply performs output and passes control to the next line.

questions.q: In what order are values bound to parameters when calling function void display(int id, double price)?
questions.hint: How are arguments matched to parameter names when calling `display(101, 19.99)`?
options: In strict left-to-right order: first value is written to id, second — to price
In reverse order: first value to price, second — to id
Order is random and depends on compiler
Values are matched by variable name matching
explanations: Correct! When calling a function, argument values are assigned to parameters strictly left-to-right: first argument to first parameter, second to second.
Incorrect. Passing order is strictly fixed by function declaration.
Incorrect. Evaluation order of arguments may vary, but binding to parameters is always left-to-right.
Incorrect. Binding occurs by position, not by name.

questions.q: Which line of code correctly saves the result of int multiply(int a, int b) into a new variable?
questions.hint: Which construct is used to assign a return value?
options: int res = multiply(3, 4);
multiply(3, 4) -> int res;
int res = int multiply(3, 4);
save multiply(3, 4) to res;
explanations: Correct! The expression `multiply(3, 4)` is evaluated and assigned to the created variable `res` via the `=` operator.
Incorrect. Such arrow syntax does not exist in C.
Incorrect. When calling a function, return type `int` before its name is not written.
Incorrect. The `save` operator does not exist in C.

questions.topic: Expressions — Calling Function Inside Math Operations
questions.q: Can a function call returning int be used directly inside a mathematical expression, for example: int result = get_number() * 2;?
questions.hint: What does a function call become after execution within expression context?
options: Yes, a function call returns a value that immediately participates in expression calculation
No, a function call must be the sole operation on a line
Yes, but only if the function is declared with inline keyword
No, a temporary variable must be declared first
explanations: Correct! Calling a value-returning function is a full-fledged expression. It is evaluated, and the substituted result participates in further operations (multiplying by 2).
Incorrect. Function calls can be freely combined in any expressions.
Incorrect. The `inline` keyword is merely a hint to the optimizer and does not affect syntax rules.
Incorrect. A temporary variable is created by the compiler automatically if needed.

questions.q: What does the static keyword placed before a function declaration do (for example, static void helper(void))?
questions.hint: Think about function visibility from other project files (modules).
options: Limits function scope to the current file (translation unit)
Forces function to execute faster due to caching
Makes all variables inside function static by default
Allows calling function without using parentheses
explanations: Correct! The `static` qualifier before a function gives it internal linkage. The function name is not exported to the linker and cannot be called from other source files (`.c`).
Incorrect. `static` affects symbol visibility to the linker, not execution speed.
Incorrect. Variables inside function retain their normal declaration rules.
Incorrect. Calling any function in C always requires `()` syntax.

questions.q: If an array is passed to function void zero_out(int arr[], int size), will its elements change in calling code when arr[0] = 0 is executed?
questions.hint: Recall what int arr[] parameter turns into when passed to a function.
options: Yes, array elements will change because array is passed via pointer to its first element
No, function is passed a local copy of entire array
A compilation error will occur, arrays cannot be modified
Will change only if array is declared with static key
explanations: Correct! Parameter `int arr[]` is equivalent to `int *arr`. A pointer to the first array element is passed, so writing to `arr[i]` modifies elements of original array in memory.
Incorrect. Arrays in C are never copied by value automatically when passed to functions.
Incorrect. Modifying array elements via pointer is standard behavior.
Incorrect. `static` is not required to modify elements.

questions.q: What is the primary goal of adding inline specifier to a small function declaration?
questions.hint: How to avoid overhead of creating stack frame and jumping to address?
options: Hint to compiler to inline function body directly at call site
Make function automatically thread-safe
Forbid function from accepting parameters
Turn function into recursive function
explanations: Correct! The `inline` keyword suggests the compiler substitute function code directly at the call point (Inlining), eliminating function call and return overhead.
Incorrect. `inline` has no effect on thread safety.
Incorrect. `inline` functions can accept any parameters.
Incorrect. Recursion and inlining are opposite concepts.

questions.topic: Data Security — Constant Pointers in Parameters
questions.q: What does declaring parameter as const int *p in function header void analyze(const int *p) guarantee?
questions.hint: Will function be able to modify value lying at address *p?
options: Function will not be able to modify value of variable pointed to by p
Function will not be able to modify address of pointer p itself
Variable in memory is completely protected against reading
Pointer p must necessarily be equal to NULL
explanations: Correct! Writing `const int *p` makes data at address `*p` read-only inside this function. Attempting to write `*p = 10` will cause a compilation error.
Incorrect. Moving pointer itself (`p++`) is allowed, as data is constant, not the pointer itself.
Incorrect. Reading data is allowed; only writing is forbidden.
Incorrect. Pointer can refer to any valid object.

questions.q: Why pass a double pointer to a function (for example, void allocate(int **ptr)) when allocating memory for an array?
questions.hint: Does address stored in original pointer itself change?
options: So function can write new address of allocated memory into caller's original pointer
To allocate memory twice as fast
This is the only syntactically valid form of calling malloc()
To forbid memory deallocation via free()
explanations: Correct! To change value of regular variable, we pass `int*`. To change value of pointer (address it points to), we must pass address of pointer itself — that is `int**`.
Incorrect. Pointer type does not affect `malloc()` speed.
Incorrect. Memory can also be allocated by returning pointer via `return` (`int* allocate()`).
Incorrect. Memory allocated on heap must be freed via `free()` in any case.

questions.q: Which of the following variants is correct syntax for declaring function pointer pfunc to a function taking int and returning double?
questions.hint: Pay attention to parentheses around name and * symbol.
options: double (*pfunc)(int);
double *pfunc(int);
double pfunc*(int);
(double*)(int) pfunc;
explanations: Correct! Parentheses `(*pfunc)` are mandatory. `double (*pfunc)(int)` declares a function pointer. Without parentheses, `double *pfunc(int)` declares a function returning `double*`.
Incorrect. `double *pfunc(int);` is prototype of function returning pointer to double.
Incorrect. Invalid C syntax.
Incorrect. Invalid syntax.

questions.q: What emergency crash will a recursive function without exit condition (base case) lead to?
questions.hint: Where are return addresses and local variables saved on each new function call?
options: Stack Overflow and program crash
Memory Leak in heap
Automatic code fix by compiler
Program will ignore extra calls and continue running
explanations: Correct! Each recursive call allocates a new frame on the stack. Without a stop condition, stack will quickly exhaust allocated memory limit, leading to Stack Overflow and process crash.
Incorrect. Heap is not used when calling functions without `malloc`.
Incorrect. Compiler does not fix infinite call logic at runtime.
Incorrect. Stack memory is limited, so function cannot be called infinitely.

questions.topic: Data Types — Passing Base Types (char, float)
questions.q: How are single char type characters passed into function void process(char c)?
questions.hint: Does passing mechanism differ for int and char?
options: By value (byte copy of numeric character code is passed to function)
By pointer to first byte of automatic string
By reference
All characters are passed only through global array
explanations: Correct! Character `char` is simply an 8-bit integer. It is passed by value, like any other base type (`int`, `float`).
Incorrect. Single `char` is not a string or pointer.
Incorrect. References do not exist in C.
Incorrect. Characters are passed in standard way via stack or registers.

questions.topic: Memory Management — Returning Address of Local Variable
questions.q: Why does function int* get_ptr(void) { int a = 10; return &a; } contain a critical error?
questions.hint: What happens to variable 'a' stack frame after exiting function?
options: Variable a memory is freed upon function exit, creating a 'dangling pointer'
Syntactically forbidden to return pointers from functions
Variable a must be zeroed out beforehand
Function is required to accept at least one argument
explanations: Correct! Local variable `a` lives on stack only while `get_ptr()` executes. Returning its address leads to a dangling pointer: accessing this memory after return causes Undefined Behavior.
Incorrect. Pointers can be returned, but must point to valid memory (heap, static, or external variables).
Incorrect. Zeroing out will not solve destruction of local stack memory.
Incorrect. Functions without arguments are completely valid.

questions.q: Why is declaration extern int calculate(int x); used in a header file?
questions.hint: Where is actual definition of such function body located?
options: Informs compiler that function is defined in another source file or library
Makes function private to current file
Automatically creates empty function body
Indicates that function should execute in separate thread
explanations: Correct! Keyword `extern` states that function has external linkage and its definition (body) is in another module/file of project.
Incorrect. `static` is used for file privacy.
Incorrect. `extern` only declares signature, but does not generate function body.
Incorrect. `extern` is not related to multithreading.
